name: Binary and denary
rule: Each bit in an 8-bit binary number has a place value: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. To turn binary into denary, add the place values that have a 1 under them. To turn denary into binary, take the biggest place value that fits, subtract it, and repeat with what is left.
trick: Write 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 above the bits before you do anything else. Most mistakes come from counting places in your head.

another.text: Binary is like paying with coins worth 128p, 64p, 32p and so on, where you can use each coin once or not at all. A 1 means you used that coin.

walkthrough.board: Convert 01010110 to denary, then convert 86 back to binary.

steps.say: Write the place values over the bits: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

steps.ask: Which place values have a 1 under them?
Now go back the other way. What is the biggest place value that fits into 86?
What is the biggest place value that fits into 22?

steps.say: So the 1s go under 64, 16, 4 and 2, giving 01010110. Both directions agree.

questions.stem: What is 00010101 in denary?
What is 40 as an 8-bit binary number?

name: Hexadecimal
sub: One hex digit is four bits
rule: Hexadecimal (base 16) uses the digits 0 to 9 and then A to F for 10 to 15. One hex digit stands for exactly four bits (a nibble). To change binary to hex, split it into nibbles and convert each one using 8, 4, 2, 1. To change two-digit hex to denary, multiply the first digit by 16 and add the second.
trick: Learn A = 10 and F = 15; the letters in between count up from there.

another.text: Hex is a shorthand, like writing a dozen instead of twelve things one by one. Four bits squash into one symbol, so a long binary number gets much shorter.

walkthrough.board: Convert 1100 1001 to hexadecimal, then to denary.

steps.say: Split the byte into two nibbles: 1100 and 1001. Each nibble becomes one hex digit.

steps.ask: Using 8, 4, 2, 1, what is 1100?
steps.hint: 8 + 4 + 0 + 0. Then A is 10, B is 11, C is 12.

steps.ask: What is 1001?
So what is the hex number?
steps.then: Keep the nibbles in the same order as the binary.

steps.ask: Now to denary: C9 = 12 × 16 + 9 = ?

questions.stem: What is the hex number 2F in denary?
What is 1110 0011 in hexadecimal?
questions.why: 1110 is 14, which is E, and 0011 is 3.

name: Binary addition and shifts
rule: Add binary right to left, like column addition. 0 + 1 = 1. 1 + 1 = 10: write 0 and carry 1. 1 + 1 + 1 = 11: write 1 and carry 1. If a carry goes past the last bit, the answer does not fit: that is overflow. Shifting left by one place doubles a number; shifting right by one place halves it, and bits that fall off the end are lost.
trick: Check every answer in denary: convert both numbers, add them, and convert your binary answer back.

another.text: In binary you are only allowed 0 and 1, so the moment a column reaches 2 it is full, like a cup that overflows into the next cup along.
another.example:
1 + 1 = 2
Too much for one column
Write 0, carry 1

steps.ask: Start with the right-hand column: 1 + 1 = ?
steps.hint: 2 is not a binary digit. 2 in binary is 10.

steps.ask: Next column: 1 + 1 + the carried 1 = ?
steps.hint: Three 1s make 3, which is 11 in binary.

steps.ask: Next column: 0 + 1 + the carried 1 = ?
Last column: 0 + 0 + the carried 1 = ?
Read the answer from left to right. 0011 + 0111 = ?
Shifting 1010 one place left gives 10100. What did that do to 10?

questions.why: 3 + 5 = 8, which is 1000. The carries ripple all the way to the left.

questions.stem: What is 00011000 shifted right by 2 places?
questions.why: Two places right divides by 4: 24 becomes 6. 01100000 is a left shift.

name: File sizes and units
rule: 8 bits make 1 byte. 1,000 bytes make a kilobyte, 1,000 KB a megabyte and 1,000 MB a gigabyte (you may also see 1,024, written KiB, MiB and GiB). Image size in bits = width × height × colour depth. Sound size in bits = sample rate × bit depth × seconds. Divide bits by 8 to get bytes.
trick: Work it out in bits first, then divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for each step up.

examples.text: n bits per pixel give 2ⁿ colours

another.text: Bits are like single sweets, bytes are bags of 8 sweets, and kilobytes are boxes of 1,000 bags. To count boxes, first count the sweets, then bag them, then box them.

walkthrough.board: A 200 × 100 pixel image has a colour depth of 4 bits. What is its size in kilobytes?

steps.ask: How many pixels are there?
steps.hint: Multiply the width by the height.

steps.ask: Each pixel needs 4 bits. How many bits for the whole image?
To turn bits into bytes, divide by what?
With 1 KB = 1,000 bytes, how many kilobytes?

questions.stem: How many bits are there in 3 bytes?
questions.why: Each byte is 8 bits, so 3 × 8 = 24.

questions.stem: A 10 × 10 pixel image uses 8 bits per pixel. What is its size in bytes?
questions.why: 100 pixels × 8 bits = 800 bits, and 800 ÷ 8 = 100 bytes. 800 is the size in bits.

name: Trace tables
sub: Run the code one line at a time
rule: A trace table has a column for each variable (and one for output) and a new row each time a value changes. Follow the code one line at a time, write down every new value as it is assigned, and check the loop condition every time round.
trick: Never run two lines in your head at once. Write each change down, even the boring ones, and the answer falls out of the last row.

examples.note: x becomes 7: write 7 in the x column
The loop body runs with i = 1, 2 and 3: three times

another.text: A trace table is like keeping score in a game: every time someone scores, you write the new total down instead of trying to remember it.

walkthrough.board: total ← 10. FOR i ← 1 TO 3: total ← total − i. ENDFOR. OUTPUT total

steps.ask: Before the loop starts, what is total?
First time round, i = 1. What does total become?
Second time round, i = 2. What does total become?
steps.hint: Take i away from the total you already have: 9 − 2.

steps.ask: Third time round, i = 3. What does total become?
Does the loop run again with i = 4?
What is output?

questions.stem: x ← 2, then x ← x × 3, then x ← x − 1. What is x now?
count ← 0. WHILE count < 3: count ← count + 1. ENDWHILE. How many times does the loop body run?
questions.why: count goes 1, 2, 3. When count is 3, count < 3 is false, so the loop stops after 3 runs.

name: AND, OR and NOT
rule: AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1. OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1. NOT flips its single input: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0. A truth table lists every combination of inputs: 2 inputs need 4 rows, and each extra input doubles that. Work out brackets first.
trick: AND is strict (both), OR is easy-going (either). Anything AND 0 is 0; anything OR 1 is 1.

another.text: AND is like needing both a ticket and a wristband to get in. OR is like being let in with either one. NOT is saying the opposite.
another.example:
Ticket AND wristband: both needed
Ticket OR wristband: one is enough
NOT raining = dry

walkthrough.board: Q = (A OR B) AND (NOT C), with A = 0, B = 1, C = 0

steps.ask: First bracket: A OR B = 0 OR 1 = ?
steps.hint: OR needs only one input to be 1.

steps.ask: Second bracket: NOT C = NOT 0 = ?
Now combine them: 1 AND 1 = ?
If C were 1 instead, what would Q be?
steps.then: NOT C would be 0, and anything AND 0 is 0.

questions.stem: What is 1 AND 0?
questions.why: AND is 1 only when both inputs are 1.

questions.stem: How many rows does a truth table for 5 inputs need?
questions.why: Each input doubles the combinations: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.

name: MOD and DIV
rule: DIV is whole-number division: it gives how many whole times one number goes into another and throws the remainder away. MOD gives the remainder that is left over. 14 DIV 4 = 3 and 14 MOD 4 = 2, because 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 are left.
trick: n MOD 2 = 0 means n is even. The answer to MOD is always smaller than the number you divide by.

another.text: Share 14 sweets between 4 friends. Each friend gets 3 (that is DIV) and 2 sweets are left in the bag (that is MOD).
another.example:
14 sweets, 4 friends
3 each: DIV
2 left over: MOD

walkthrough.board: mins ← 135. hours ← mins DIV 60. left ← mins MOD 60. OUTPUT hours, left

steps.say: DIV keeps the whole part of a division. MOD keeps what is left over.

steps.ask: How many whole times does 60 go into 135?
steps.hint: 60, 120, 180: which is the last one that fits inside 135?

steps.ask: 2 lots of 60 is 120. How much of 135 is left over?
What is output?
Which test tells you a number n is even?
steps.then: An even number leaves no remainder when it is divided by 2.

questions.stem: What is 19 MOD 4?
questions.why: 4 × 4 = 16, and 19 − 16 = 3 left over. 4 would be 19 DIV 4.

questions.stem: What is 26 DIV 6?
questions.why: 6 goes into 26 four whole times (24). The 2 left over would be 26 MOD 6.

name: Translators
rule: A CPU can only run machine code. A high-level language such as Python is written for people, so it must be translated first. A compiler translates the whole program at once into a file that can be run. An interpreter translates and runs one line at a time and stops at the first error. An assembler turns assembly language, a low-level language written in mnemonics, into machine code.
trick: Compiler: the whole book is translated before anyone reads it. Interpreter: it is translated out loud, one sentence at a time.

examples.text: A game sold as a file that is ready to run
examples.note: Compiled: it runs fast and the source code stays hidden

examples.text: Testing a program you are still writing
examples.note: Interpreted: it stops at the line with the error

another.text: Imagine your friend only reads French. You could translate your whole letter first and post the French copy (a compiler), or sit beside them and translate each sentence as they go (an interpreter).
another.example:
Whole letter first: compiler
Sentence by sentence: interpreter

walkthrough.board: A student writes a program in Python, tests it, then wants to give friends a file they can run.

steps.ask: Can the CPU run the Python code as it is written?
options: No, it must be translated into machine code
steps.hint: A CPU only understands binary machine code.

steps.ask: While testing, the student wants the program to stop at the line with the error. Which translator does that?
steps.then: It translates and runs one line at a time, so earlier lines have already run.

steps.ask: The friends should get one file that runs with no translator installed. Which translator makes that?
steps.then: A compiler translates everything up front into an executable file.

steps.ask: Another program is written in mnemonics such as LDA and ADD. What translates it?

questions.stem: Which translator turns the whole program into machine code before it is run?
questions.why: A compiler translates everything at once. An interpreter goes line by line, and an assembler is for assembly language.

questions.stem: Which of these is a low-level language?
questions.why: Assembly language is close to machine code and is written for one type of processor. Python and Java are high-level languages.

name: Counting from 0
sub: Array and string positions start at 0
rule: In GCSE pseudocode the first item in an array is at index 0, not 1, and the first character of a string is at position 0. So an array of 5 items uses indexes 0 to 4, and the last index is always one less than the length. A two-dimensional array is read as grid[row][column], and both start at 0.
trick: Write the index numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 above the items before you look anything up. To find item n counting normally, use index n − 1.

examples.note: Index 0 is cat, so index 1 is dog
P is 0, L is 1, so A is 2

another.text: Think of the floors in a UK lift. You get in on the ground floor, which is 0, and the next one up is floor 1. Arrays count the same way: the first item sits on floor 0.
another.example:
Ground floor: 0
One floor up: 1
The 4th floor you visit: 3

walkthrough.board: colours ← ["red", "blue", "green", "pink"]. OUTPUT colours[2], then OUTPUT colours[LEN(colours) − 1]

steps.say: Number the items from 0: red is 0, blue is 1, green is 2, pink is 3.

steps.ask: What is colours[2]?
LEN(colours) is the number of items. What is it?
So LEN(colours) − 1 is 3. What is colours[3]?
steps.then: The last index is always the length minus 1.

steps.ask: What would colours[4] do?
options: Cause an error: there is no index 4
steps.then: Four items use indexes 0 to 3, so 4 is past the end.

questions.stem: days ← ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"]. What is days[3]?
questions.why: Mon is 0, Tue is 1, Wed is 2, so index 3 is Thu.

questions.stem: An array holds 8 items. What is the index of the last item?
questions.why: Indexes start at 0, so 8 items use 0 to 7.

name: High-level and low-level
sub: Written for people or close to the CPU
rule: A high-level language such as Python uses English-like words, so it is easier to read, write and debug, and the same program can run on different types of computer once it is translated. A low-level language (machine code or assembly language) is close to what the CPU does: it is written for one type of processor, it is hard to read, but it gives direct control of the hardware and memory and can run very fast in very little memory.
trick: High-level is good for people. Low-level is good for the machine. Ask which one the question cares about.

examples.text: A school writes an app for laptops and tablets
examples.note: High-level: quicker to write and works on both types of computer

examples.text: Code for a tiny chip in a washing machine with very little memory
examples.note: Low-level: small, fast and controls the hardware directly

another.text: A high-level language is like giving a taxi driver an address. A low-level language is like telling them every single turn of the wheel yourself. The second is harder, but you control exactly what happens.
another.example:
"Take me to the station": high-level
"Left, 20 metres, right...": low-level

walkthrough.board: Two jobs: (1) a quiz app for phones and laptops, (2) code for a heart monitor chip that must react instantly and has tiny memory.

steps.say: High-level languages are easier for people. Low-level languages give control of the hardware.

steps.ask: For the quiz app, what matters most?
options: It is quick to write and runs on different devices
steps.hint: Phones and laptops have different processors.
steps.line: Job 1 needs: easy to write, portable

steps.ask: So which kind of language suits job 1?
steps.then: Once translated, the same high-level code can run on different machines.

steps.ask: The heart monitor has tiny memory and must be very fast. Which suits it?
steps.then: Low-level code can be small and fast and talks to the hardware directly.

steps.ask: What is the main downside of low-level code?
options: It is hard to read and only works on one type of processor
steps.line: Downside: hard to read, not portable

questions.stem: Why is a high-level language easier to debug?
options: It uses English-like words that people can read
It runs directly on the CPU
questions.why: High-level code is written for people, so mistakes are easier to spot. It still has to be translated before the CPU can run it.

questions.stem: Why might a programmer choose a low-level language?
options: So the program runs on any computer
So the code is shorter to write
questions.why: Low-level code gives direct control of the processor and memory. It only works on one type of processor and takes longer to write.

name: IDE tools
rule: An IDE (integrated development environment) is one program with the tools for writing code. The editor has line numbers, colour-coded keywords (syntax highlighting) and auto-indent. Error diagnostics point to the line with a mistake. A run-time environment lets you run and test the program. Debugging tools include breakpoints, which pause the program at a chosen line, stepping, which runs one line at a time, and watching variables to see their values.
trick: Writing the code: editor tools. Finding the mistake: error messages, breakpoints, stepping and watched variables.

examples.text: The keyword IF turns blue as you type it
examples.note: Syntax highlighting, part of the editor

examples.text: The program stops at line 12 so you can check total

another.text: An IDE is like a pencil case made for coding. The pen writes (the editor), the ruler checks your lines (error messages), and the magnifying glass lets you look closely at one bit (the debugger).
another.example:
Write: editor
Check: error messages
Look closely: breakpoint

walkthrough.board: A program gives the wrong total. The programmer wants to stop it at line 8 and see what total holds.

steps.say: An IDE has tools for writing code and tools for finding mistakes.

steps.ask: Which tool pauses the program at line 8?
steps.hint: Which tool is about stopping the program?

steps.ask: While it is paused, how can they see the value of total?
They want to run the next lines one at a time. What is that called?
steps.line: One line at a time: stepping

steps.ask: A missing bracket is underlined in red before the program runs. Which tool did that?
steps.then: Error diagnostics spot mistakes and say which line they are on.

questions.stem: Which IDE feature colours keywords so code is easier to read?
questions.why: Syntax highlighting is an editor tool. A breakpoint pauses a running program.

questions.stem: What does stepping through a program do?
options: Runs it one line at a time
questions.why: Stepping runs one line at a time so you can follow what the program does.
